repos.title: MemT-1.0: Towards Memory-Native Evolution
repos.paper_summary:
MemT-1.0 is a family of memory foundation models that keep history inside the model's computation rather than in an external context window or retrieval store. The released models are MemT-1.0-Nano (36B parameters, 3B activated, 10M dynamic memory) and MemT-1.0-Flash (288B parameters, 17B activated, 336M dynamic memory). It builds on the earlier Metis model, replacing token selection with a token-level update based on Gated DeltaNet-2 and adding Mixture-of-Storage to scale memory capacity. Training is continued pre-training followed by post-training on 34B tokens.

Across 11 memory benchmarks, the models outperform parametric memory baselines on average and remain competitive with retrieval-augmented methods, while largely preserving general capabilities under the noise setting. At a 128K-token history, Nano reaches about 1.86× end-to-end inference speedup and a 66× reduction in persistent storage relative to a full-context KV cache. On SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Multilingual, internalized experience improves average task success over agents without experience.

The memory state is fixed-size, so its capacity is bounded and precise recall may degrade as history grows.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: MemT-1.0 upgrades the Metis memory design and releases 36B and 288B parameter models with Mixture-of-Storage.

digest_headlines.heading: Model Architecture
digest_headlines.headline: Native memory runs as a parallel attention branch in selected Transformer blocks, with backbone layers left unchanged.

digest_headlines.heading: Training
digest_headlines.headline: Backbone preparation and a two-stage pipeline train memory by distilling from a frozen full-context teacher on 34B tokens.

digest_headlines.heading: System and Infrastructure
digest_headlines.headline: Windowed execution of Mixture-of-Storage cuts peak memory by 80.1% for a 32K-token pack, adding 1.6% to forward-backward time.

digest_headlines.heading: Memory Scaling Behavior
digest_headlines.headline: Memory score rises from 36.65 to 46.80 over two post-training epochs, and four experts beat two by up to 2.69 points.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Native memory averages 50.6 on memory benchmarks for Flash and 47.0 for Nano, ahead of parametric baselines but behind textual systems.

digest_headlines.heading: Application in Agentic Tasks
digest_headlines.headline: Stored procedural experience raises the coding benchmark success rate from 66.07% to 69.33% without experience text in context.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations and Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: A fixed-size memory state limits recall of detail, and the relation between local and hyper memory remains unresolved.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: MemT-1.0 outperforms the evaluated parametric baselines on average, preserves general capabilities under noise, and points to future memory scaling.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix gives author lists, memory configurations, projection and gate initialization, training settings, and a stability bound for the update.

repos.title: SkillOpt: Executive Strategy for Self-Evolving Agent Skills
repos.paper_summary: SkillOpt is a text-space optimizer that trains one agent skill document, a natural-language procedure added to the context of a frozen target model. A separate frontier optimizer model reads scored rollouts from a training split and proposes add, delete, or replace edits. A candidate skill is kept only if it raises the score on a held-out selection split. Stability controls include a cap on edits per step (the "textual learning rate"), a buffer of rejected edits passed to later reflection calls, and an epoch-wise slow/meta update. The paper reports results on six benchmarks, seven target models, and three execution modes (direct chat, Codex, Claude Code). For GPT–5.5 in direct chat, the average gain over no skill is +23.5 points, and the average margin over the strongest per-cell baseline is +5.4 points. Exported skills are 300–2,000 tokens, built from 11–44 accepted edits. The paper also reports transfer across model scales and harnesses, and to Omni-MATH. Limitations: the method optimizes one skill for one domain, and it depends on a separate frontier optimizer model. The provided text ends before the slow/meta update is described, so that component and its ablation results are not covered here.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: SkillOpt optimizes an agent's skill document as external state, with validation-gated edits and no weight updates.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior skill work mainly builds or evolves skill libraries, while prompt optimizers target prompts rather than a persistent skill.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Each step edits the skill with bounded add, delete and replace operations, accepted only if held-out selection score strictly improves.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: SkillOpt is best or tied on all 52 evaluated cells, lifting GPT–5.5 by 23.5 points in direct chat.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Compact skills optimized this way transfer across model scales, harnesses and a nearby benchmark without weight updates.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists the optimizer prompt contracts, limitations, and experimental protocol with patch and split details.

repos.title: RadixFlow: Filling Execution Bubbles in Prefix-Cached Hybrid LLM Serving
repos.paper_summary: RadixFlow is a batch-construction policy for prefix-cached serving of hybrid LLMs, where a matched prefix may need recurrent state still being produced in the same round. Its state-ready traversal blocks only the consumer of that dependency, puts it in a wait queue for the next round, and keeps scanning for independent branches that fit. The paper proves that, for a fixed round and native order, the batch contains every branch that prefix-stop would select, and that no avoidable bubble remains when readiness is monotone and no other failure stops the scan. On five hybrid models, evaluated on QuALITY and RACE candidate-scoring workloads in vLLM on A800 GPUs, it lowers mean latency by 3% to 24% and worker rounds by 11% to 44% versus the native Radix scheduler, with prefix reuse within 0.03 percentage points. On the full-attention Qwen3-8B control, latency is unchanged at 16.4 s. Ablations attribute most of the gain on larger Qwen3.5 models to traversal. The authors state that evaluation covers one generated token under fixed arrival settings, and that heavier per-round cost reduces how much of the round saving reaches latency.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Hybrid LLMs make a cache-matched branch wait for a same-round producer, and the native scan stalls behind it.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prefix-caching systems decide what state can be reused, while RadixFlow changes only which executable branches a round selects.

digest_headlines.heading: Problem Formulation
digest_headlines.headline: Batch construction must admit only branches with a matching prefix, usable state at the resume boundary, and fitting resources.

digest_headlines.heading: RadixFlow
digest_headlines.headline: RadixFlow blocks only the consumer of a same-round dependency and keeps scanning for independent work that fits.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: RadixFlow lowers mean latency and worker rounds on the hybrid models while prefix reuse stays nearly unchanged.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: A cache match is not yet a runnable branch, so schedulers should separate same-round dependencies from memory pressure.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Results cover candidate-conditioned prefill with one generated token under frozen settings, without load sweeps or production traces.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethical Considerations
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments use public benchmark inputs and public model weights, and the paper discloses assistance used in implementation and revision.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers design rationale, replay protocol, timing semantics, stream proofs, and audits of baselines and output agreement.

repos.title: Reinforcement Learning for Versatile, Dynamic, and Robust Bipedal Locomotion Control
repos.paper_summary: This paper presents a dual-history reinforcement learning controller for bipedal robots, enabling diverse locomotion skills including walking, running, and jumping on the Cassie robot. The method uses a long-term input/output history encoder to adapt to dynamics changes and contact events, combined with a short-term history fed directly to the policy network to handle high-frequency control needs. Training follows a three-stage curriculum: single-task learning, task randomization, and dynamics randomization. In simulation ablations, the dual-history architecture outperforms baselines like RMA and state-feedback-only policies under randomized dynamics parameters. Real-world experiments demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, with the robot maintaining stable standing for 459 days, completing a 400-meter dash, and executing jumps up to 1.4 meters forward and 0.44 meters high. The authors identify task randomization as a key source of robustness distinct from dynamics randomization, promoting compliant recovery behaviors. Limitations include difficulty achieving precise velocity tracking during fast running and the requirement for specific reference motions; for instance, backward jumps could not be learned from a forward-jumping reference alone.

repos.title: The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery
repos.paper_summary: The Agentic Scientist is a scaffold that runs coding agents through a computational research campaign, from task specification to manuscript. A drafting pipeline turns a research brief into an initial program, evaluators, and a task contract. Parallel workers run research cycles in which an ideation agent writes a structured hypothesis with target rubrics and an execution agent tests it within a fixed budget. Workers share distilled memory at cycle boundaries. The selected program then gets controlled baselines, ablations, and post-hoc analysis, and a writer agent drafts a LaTeX paper that an audit agent checks against the results. A meta-trained evolution strategy matches or exceeds CMA-ES on 5 of 7 unseen Brax tasks. An Error Diffusion paper produced with the system was accepted at ALIFE 2026. Across 70 campaigns, higher search scores predict higher AI reviewer scores on 4 of 5 tasks. The autoillustrate figure tool scores 37.5 against 25.0 for PaperBanana on PaperBananaBench. Limitations: the metric is an AI-reviewer proxy, only one paper had external review, task drafting is unreliable for larger tasks, and evaluation covers only computational machine learning.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: The paper introduces The Agentic Scientist, a scaffold that lets human researchers run end-to-end computational research with coding agents.

digest_headlines.heading: Background & Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Existing AI scientist systems cover parts of the research loop, but lack a reusable orchestration and evidence layer.

digest_headlines.heading: The Agentic Scientist: An Orchestration Layer for Research Agents
digest_headlines.headline: The scaffold runs task drafting, parallel investigation with contracted cycles, retrospective ablations, and grounded paper writing with audit.

digest_headlines.heading: AI Co-Scientist and Conference Paper Submission
digest_headlines.headline: A single paper written with the system was accepted at ALIFE 2026 after human verification and manual edits.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluating The Agentic Scientist Across Tasks, Harnesses, and LLMs
digest_headlines.headline: Across 70 campaigns, final task performance was positively associated with AI reviewer scores on four of five tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Additional Case Studies: Putting The Agentic Scientist to work
digest_headlines.headline: Search raised multi-needle retrieval accuracy to 98.0% and reinforcement-learning fine-tuning validation accuracy to about 71.9%, with evolution-strategy results mixed.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluating autoillustrate on PaperBananaBench
digest_headlines.headline: autoillustrate scored 37.5 overall against 25.0 for the best PaperBanana variant, below the human reference of 50.0.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Coding agents can contribute to research in an orchestrated workflow, but unstated specifications, proxy metrics and narrow domains limit the evidence.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers related work, per-task discoveries, CMA-ES and Error Diffusion results, experimental protocols, and figure examples.

repos.title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity
repos.paper_summary: The Switch Transformer replaces the standard feed-forward layer in Transformers with a sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) module that routes each token to a single expert, reducing communication overhead and improving training stability. By using top-1 routing instead of top-k, the model maintains constant computational cost per token while scaling parameter count. The paper introduces selective precision casting to stabilize bfloat16 training and an auxiliary load-balancing loss to ensure uniform expert usage. Experiments on the C4 corpus show that a 64-expert Switch-Base model achieves the same pre-training quality as T5-Base in one-seventh the time. Fine-tuning results indicate consistent improvements over T5-Base and T5-Large on GLUE, SuperGLUE, SQuAD, and summarization tasks. Distilling these sparse models into dense T5-Base architectures preserves approximately 30% of the quality gain while compressing model size by up to 99%. In multilingual settings across 101 languages, the method yields a mean 5x speedup over mT5-Base. A limitation is that distillation does not fully recover teacher performance, and the approach relies on specific hardware parallelism strategies for trillion-parameter scales.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Sparse expert routing is proposed to add parameters without raising per-example compute, with gains across pre-training, fine-tuning and multilingual training.

digest_headlines.heading: Switch Transformer
digest_headlines.headline: Routing each token to one expert simplifies Mixture of Experts, with capacity limits and a balancing loss keeping training stable.

digest_headlines.heading: Scaling Properties
digest_headlines.headline: Increasing experts at fixed FLOPS per token speeds up pre-training, with Switch-Base 64 reaching T5-Base quality in one-seventh the time.

digest_headlines.heading: Downstream Results
digest_headlines.headline: Switch models improve most T5 fine-tuning tasks, distill to dense models keeping 30% of gains, and beat mT5 on all 101 languages.

digest_headlines.heading: Designing Models with Data, Model, and Expert-Parallelism
digest_headlines.headline: Data, model and expert parallelism combine to train 395 billion and 1.6 trillion parameter Switch models, with Switch-XXL sometimes unstable.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work scales models through model parallelism and conditional computation, including mixture of experts and attention sparsity.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Sparse models are argued to outperform dense models per step and on wall clock time, but distilled versions keep only about 30% of gains.

digest_headlines.heading: Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: Remaining challenges include stabilizing the largest models, heterogeneous experts, expert layers beyond feed-forward layers, and other modalities.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Switch Transformers are presented as stable, sample-efficient language learners across pre-training, fine-tuning and multi-task training.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix covers attention Switch layers, token rerouting, router exploration, small-scale results, upstream-downstream correlation and pseudocode.

repos.title: FinRL: A Deep Reinforcement Learning Library for Automated Stock Trading in Quantitative Finance
repos.paper_summary:
FinRL is an open-source Python library for automated stock trading using deep reinforcement learning. It structures the workflow into three layers: a market environment simulator, a set of pre-configured DRL agents, and application modules for single-stock, multi-stock, and portfolio allocation tasks. The environment layer models trading as a Markov Decision Process using historical data from six indices (NASDAQ-100, DJIA, S&P 500, HSI, SSE 50, CSI 300) at daily, hourly, or minute granularity. Agents include DQN, DDPG, PPO, SAC, A2C, and TD3, built on OpenAI Baselines and Stable Baselines.

The library incorporates market frictions such as transaction costs, bid-ask spreads, and a turbulence index to control risk during extreme volatility. Backtesting uses the `pyfolio` package. In demonstrations over 2019–2020 data, PPO-based single-stock strategies achieved Sharpe ratios between 1.10 and 1.49, outperforming the S&P 500 baseline of 0.74. For DJIA constituents, TD3 and DDPG strategies yielded Sharpe ratios of 1.38 and 1.28, respectively, exceeding the min-variance baseline of 0.44. Limitations include reliance on historical data that may not reflect future market regimes and the computational cost of training multiple agent configurations.

repos.title: Step-DPO: Step-wise Preference Optimization for Long-chain Reasoning of LLMs
repos.paper_summary:
Step-DPO is a preference optimization method for large language models that treats individual reasoning steps, rather than full answers, as the unit of comparison to improve mathematical reasoning. The method modifies the standard Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) objective by conditioning on preceding correct steps and optimizing the probability of the next correct step versus the first erroneous step. This allows the model to pinpoint specific errors in long chains of thought without penalizing earlier correct logic.

The authors construct a dataset of 10K preference pairs using a three-step pipeline: collecting incorrect model outputs, localizing the first error, and sampling self-generated corrections from the reference model. They find that using in-distribution data generated by the model itself yields better results than out-of-distribution data written by humans or GPT-4. On the MATH benchmark, applying Step-DPO to Qwen2-72B-Instruct increases accuracy from 69.4% to 70.8%, while GSM8K accuracy rises from 92.4% to 94.0%. These gains are achieved with fewer than 500 training steps. The approach also improves performance on competition-level problems like AIME 2024, where Qwen2-72B-Instruct scores 4/30 compared to 5/30 for the base instruct model.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Vanilla DPO cannot locate errors in long math reasoning, so Step-DPO compares individual reasoning steps instead.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Works
digest_headlines.headline: Prior methods improve math reasoning through prompting, data augmentation or reinforcement learning, but each has stated limits.

digest_headlines.heading: Step-DPO
digest_headlines.headline: Step-DPO builds preference pairs from the first wrong step, with the model's own correct continuation as the preferred choice.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Step-DPO raises Qwen2-72B-Instruct to 70.8% on MATH, with approximately a 3% boost for models above 70B.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude Step-DPO with 10K pairs gives significant gains, particularly for large models.

repos.title: OpenCollab: A Multi-Agent Coding Framework with Programmable Collaboration and Controllable Runtime
repos.paper_summary:
OpenCollab is a multi-agent coding framework that decouples organizational orchestration from a shared execution runtime to enable controlled evaluation of agent collaboration. It introduces Adherence, a metric quantifying whether agents follow their declared topology, and uses the complier average causal effect (CACE) to attribute performance gains to actual collaboration. The system enforces identical budgets, tools, and context policies across experimental arms via pre-call admission gates and structured event streams.

Experiments on SWE-bench Pro, Terminal-Bench 2.1, and DeepSWE show OpenCollab (Duo) achieves the highest Pass@1 rates: 68.91%, 83.15%, and 65.49% respectively, outperforming Mini-SWE-agent, OpenHands, Codex CLI, and Claude Code. Single-dimension ablations reveal that changing model, tool access, budget, or topology shifts Adherence from 47.2% to 97.2%. For instance, restricting lead agents to read-only tools increases Adherence to 94.4% by forcing delegation. The paper proves that under mean exclusion, CACE identifies the configuration-level effect among adherent runs; without this restriction, the Wald ratio deviates by $(1-\alpha_{\mathrm{adh}})/\alpha_{\mathrm{adh}}$ times the non-adherent contrast. Limitations include the reliance on the untestable mean exclusion assumption for causal claims and high token costs in Duo mode, which runs two full solving processes per task.

digest_headlines.heading: 1 Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Configured multi-agent teams often fail to collaborate as declared, so benchmarks cannot show whether an organization helps.

digest_headlines.heading: 2 Motivation
digest_headlines.headline: Configured teams often collapse into single-agent loops, and prompt or log-filtering fixes introduce bias.

digest_headlines.heading: 3 Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: OpenCollab separates a shared runtime from controllers, gates limits before each call, and scores runs from event streams.

digest_headlines.heading: 4 Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Duo scores highest on all three benchmarks, and single-dimension ablations move Adherence between 47.2% and 97.2%.

digest_headlines.heading: 5 Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior studies report mixed returns from multi-agent systems, yet platforms rarely verify that the assigned organization ran.

digest_headlines.heading: 6 Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: OpenCollab decouples design from execution, so collaboration can be verified and its gains attributed under stated assumptions.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix gives identification theory for the complier average causal effect, a sensitivity analysis, paired diagnostics, reporting requirements and adherence axes.
